place.name: Statesville, North Carolina
place.county: Iredell County (Statesville is the county seat, in central Iredell)
place.coordinates: 35.784 N, -80.872 W (city); normals station 35.810 N, -80.881 W
place.elevation_note: Wikipedia gives 850 ft / 260 m for the city; NOAA lists the Statesville 2 NNE normals station at 244.8 m; other sites give 278-283 m. Terrain in town spans roughly 200-300 m.
place.physiography: Western Piedmont of North Carolina; rolling uplands drained by Fourth Creek (north side) and Third Creek (south side), which run east to the South Yadkin River.
place.brushy_mountains: An isolated southwest-northeast spur of the Blue Ridge, split from it by the Yadkin River valley, running through Caldwell, Alexander, Wilkes, Iredell and Yadkin counties. Highest point Pores Knob (2,680 ft / 820 m) in Wilkes County. The range lies to the northwest of Statesville; distance to Pores Knob is roughly 40 km NW (UNCERTAIN: my own estimate from approximate coordinates, not from a source).
place.blue_ridge: The main Blue Ridge front lies further northwest beyond the Yadkin valley (UNCERTAIN: no sourced distance found; very roughly 70-80 km by my estimate).
place.hardiness_zone_note: phzmapi.org is an unofficial API built on the 2023 USDA/PRISM data; PlantMaps still labels Statesville 7b (likely the 2012 map). Confirm at planthardiness.ars.usda.gov. Neighbouring Piedmont towns moved 7b->8a in 2023.
place.water_bodies: Lake Norman (Catawba River reservoir) lies in southern Iredell County near Mooresville, south of Statesville (UNCERTAIN: not checked against a source in this pass). The South Yadkin River drains the city's creeks.
place.climate_type: Humid subtropical (Koppen Cfa); Wikipedia notes Statesville runs somewhat cooler than much of the Piedmont due to its elevation.

normals.frost_free_days_approx: about 192 (computed from the two median dates)

soils.summary: Iredell County uplands are a mix of red-clay Piedmont soils on felsic rock (Cecil and its kin) and dark-rock (diabase/gabbro) soils such as Iredell, Mecklenburg and Lloyd. The Iredell soil series itself was first described near Statesville in 1901.
soils.dominant_series_note: UNCERTAIN: the county-wide dominance ranking was not verified. The 1964 USDA SCS 'Soil Survey of Iredell County' (Cawthorn and Jenkins) exists but its association map was not read; Web Soil Survey was not queried. Series listed below are documented as Piedmont/Iredell-area soils in the official series descriptions.

series.name: Cecil
series.note: NC state soil. Deep, well drained, red (10R-2.5YR) clay to clay-loam subsoil over felsic igneous/metamorphic saprolite; strongly to moderately acid unless limed (about pH 4.5-6.5 surface, 4.5-5.5 subsoil); erodes readily. Associated with Lloyd (redder, from mixed rock), Appling (yellower subsoil).

series.name: Iredell
series.note: Named from the Statesville area (established 1901). Moderately well drained but very slowly permeable; subsoil is dense high-shrink-swell clay (roughly 40-85% clay) from diabase/gabbro-type rock; surface strongly acid to neutral, subsoil moderately acid to mildly alkaline. Poor apple ground: water perches on the clay.

series.name: Mecklenburg
series.note: Very deep, from mafic (diabase) parent rock; associated with Cecil, Lloyd, Iredell and Pacolet; seasonal water table below 60 in.

series.name: Lloyd
series.note: Dark-red (rhodic) clay soil from mixed felsic/mafic rock; named as associated with Cecil, Mecklenburg and Iredell. Detailed description not read.

series.name: Pacolet
series.note: Like Cecil but with a thinner clay subsoil; listed as associated with Mecklenburg. Detailed description not read.

soils.typical_pH: Native soils acid (Cecil pH ~4.5-6.5); NC State targets pH 6.0-6.5 for tree fruit and advises working lime 16-18 in deep before planting, based on a soil test.
soils.texture_drainage: Red clay subsoils under a thin loamy topsoil; Cecil-type ridges drain well, but Iredell-type clays on diabase drain very slowly.

apple_implications.note: Soil-test at 1-8 in and 8-16 in, then mix lime and nutrients down to at least 18 in before planting; choose a well-drained spot; drip irrigation suits the heavy Piedmont clays.
Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds; MM.106 has very low crown-rot resistance (avoid on wet clay).
Phytophthora crown/collar rot is worst in low, heavy, poorly drained spots; avoid susceptible rootstocks there and keep the graft union above the soil line (non-NC source).
Cecil-type soils are prone to erosion, which limits their prime-farmland rating; mulch/sod on slopes.

history.fact: Statesville's leaders began building rail links in the 1830s; in the 19th century the city became a state leader in tobacco and whiskey and a major distribution centre for medicinal roots and herbs. No source found tying Statesville to apple shipping or apple nurseries.
Alexander County (the Taylorsville/Brushy Mountain apple county next door) was carved in 1847 partly from Iredell County.
The Alexander Railroad short line runs between Taylorsville and Statesville, connecting with Norfolk Southern at Statesville (from search summary of the Taylorsville town site; not opened directly).
A 1936 North Wilkesboro Journal-Patriot report put bearing apple trees in Wilkes and Alexander counties at about 600,000 (UNCERTAIN: seen only in a search-result snippet of the digitised newspaper).
Brushy Mountain growers formed the Brushy Mountain Apple Growing Co-op in 1957 (UNCERTAIN: from a search snippet of an Elon University student blog; page could not be loaded).
NC State ran a Brushy Mountains Apple Research Laboratory under the NC Agricultural Experiment Station (photo record; dates not checked).

The Brushies' orchards benefit from a thermal belt: slopes lose less heat on spring nights, so frost risk is lower than in the valleys. One family there (Perry Lowe) has grown apples since the early 1900s.
Taylorsville (Alexander County) calls itself 'Apple Town', puts an apple tree on the county seal, and holds an Apple Blossom Festival in May and an Apple Festival in October (from search summary).
The Brushy Mountain Apple Festival, run by the Brushy Mountain Ruritan Club, fills downtown North Wilkesboro on the first Saturday of October; founded 1978 per Wikipedia (some sources say 1975).

Regional nursery context: NC's first documented nursery was Abijah Pinson's at Westfield, Surry County (1806); Cedar Cove Nursery in Yadkin County (from 1874) offered ~60 apple varieties by the early 1900s. Pores Knob Nursery in Wilkes County sold apples in the early 1900s; Catawba County Nursery (1890 catalogue) and Startown Nursery, Newton (1902) also sold apples.
Before nurseries, NC farmers commonly propagated a good apple by digging and replanting root sprouts; seedling orchards were slowly replaced by grafted trees in the 1800s.

pests_diseases.name: Bitter rot / Glomerella leaf spot and fruit rot
pests_diseases.note: Colletotrichum summer rots are a top NC problem; Golden Delicious offspring (Gala, Golden Delicious, Pink Lady, Jonagold) are most susceptible; NC programs start at petal fall and repeat every 7-14 days to harvest; scouting from late May.

pests_diseases.name: Summer rots generally
pests_diseases.note: NC State's gardener handbook calls summer rots the most serious apple disease in NC, with no resistant cultivars.

pests_diseases.name: White rot (Botryosphaeria dothidea)
pests_diseases.note: Sunken fruit rot reaching the core plus orange bark cankers. No NC State page read; general description from Minnesota Extension. Listed in NC State's Piedmont heirloom guide only as 'black rot'.

pests_diseases.name: Fire blight
pests_diseases.note: Bacterial; warm (~65 F) humid weather at bloom and rain spread it; Gala and Pink Lady highly susceptible; prune 12 in below dead tissue in dry winter weather; Geneva rootstocks resist it; M.26 very low resistance.

pests_diseases.name: Cedar-apple rust
pests_diseases.note: Needs both apple and eastern red cedar/juniper; causes leaf spots and early fruit drop; prevention by resistant cultivars and timed fungicides; hard to sustain where cedars are common.

pests_diseases.name: Sooty blotch and flyspeck
pests_diseases.note: Cosmetic surface fungi, a problem in the humid Southeast without sprays; favoured by 61-84 F and long wet periods; prune to open canopy, remove mummies, manage hedgerows.

pests_diseases.name: Apple scab, black rot, powdery mildew
pests_diseases.note: Listed among Piedmont apple diseases; scab/rust resistant cultivars help.

pests_diseases.name: Phytophthora crown/collar rot
pests_diseases.note: Worst on heavy, poorly drained soil and low spots; avoid susceptible rootstocks (MM.106 very low crown-rot resistance per NC State) and do not bury the graft union.

pests_diseases.name: Codling moth
pests_diseases.note: Larvae bore into fruit; sanitation, bagging, traps, sprays at egg hatch; late varieties less hit.

pests_diseases.name: Plum curculio
pests_diseases.note: Scars young fruit; jar the tree over a tarp in early morning and pick up drops.

pests_diseases.name: Brown marmorated stink bug
pests_diseases.note: Invasive; a leading late-season apple pest in NC; feeding spots resemble hail or bitter pit; samurai wasp is a natural enemy.

pests_diseases.name: Oriental fruit moth, Japanese beetle
pests_diseases.note: NOT VERIFIED: no NC State apple-specific source found in this pass.

pests_diseases.name: Late frost after early bloom
pests_diseases.note: Apples bloom with the dogwoods in the Piedmont; closed buds survive ~20-23 F but open bloom is hurt at ~27-28 F; site on slopes with air drainage, avoid frost pockets.

pests_diseases.name: Heat at harvest
pests_diseases.note: NC State maturity monitoring reported cultivars ripening 7-14 days early in a hot season, with heat and humidity complicating harvest; red colour develops poorly in warm regions.

pests_diseases.name: Deer
pests_diseases.note: NOT VERIFIED: no Piedmont-specific source gathered.

varieties.name: Redfree, Prima, Priscilla, Jonafree
varieties.why: NC State lists them as resistant to one or more of scab, mildew, cedar-apple rust, fire blight.

varieties.name: Gala, Fuji, Golden Delicious, Red Delicious
varieties.why: Caswell County (NC Piedmont) Extension's suggested Piedmont apples.

varieties.name: Lee Calhoun heirloom list (see heirlooms)

varieties.name: Enterprise, Liberty, GoldRush, Pristine, Crimson Crisp
varieties.why: NOT VERIFIED for NC by an NC source in this pass; Kentucky recommends Enterprise/Liberty/Priscilla/WineCrisp, and NC State says Liberty performs poorly in NC.

avoid.name: Liberty
avoid.why: NC State: disease resistant but performs poorly in North Carolina.

avoid.name: Gala, Pink Lady, Golden Delicious, Jonagold (in low-spray plantings)
avoid.why: Highly susceptible to Glomerella/bitter rot; Gala and Pink Lady also highly susceptible to fire blight.

avoid.name: Honeycrisp
avoid.why: UNCERTAIN: no NC State source found on heat performance; general literature says it is very prone to bitter pit and colours poorly in heat.

rootstocks.name: Seedling
rootstocks.note: Full size, bears in 6-10 yr; medium crown-rot, high fire-blight resistance.

rootstocks.name: MM.111
rootstocks.note: ~85% size, bears 4-6 yr, medium crown-rot resistance, low fire-blight resistance; NC State Chatham guide gives ~14-16 ft semi-dwarf. Reasonable on clay.

rootstocks.name: MM.106
rootstocks.note: ~80% size, very low crown-rot resistance: avoid on wet Piedmont clay.

rootstocks.name: M.7(a)
rootstocks.note: ~70% size, medium crown rot, high fire-blight resistance (per NC State table); ~12-14 ft.

rootstocks.name: M.26
rootstocks.note: ~50% size, very low fire-blight resistance; needs staking; poor on badly drained sites.

rootstocks.name: M.9 / Mark / Bud.9
rootstocks.note: ~35% size (8-10 ft), low fire-blight resistance, permanent staking/trellis.

rootstocks.name: Geneva series (G.41, G.935, etc.)
rootstocks.note: Bred for fire-blight and crown-rot resistance; NC State fire blight page recommends G-series; G.41/G.935 ratings from Cornell/Penn State trials (non-NC).

grower_notes.note: Piedmont apples bloom about with the dogwoods; harvest runs June to November depending on variety (early June-July, mid Aug-Sept, late Oct-Nov).
Plant at least two varieties with overlapping bloom; triploids give no good pollen; crabapples make good pollinizers; avoid insecticides during bloom.
Chill hours are not a concern for apples anywhere in NC.
Median last 32 F frost at Statesville is about April 16 and first fall frost about October 25 (1991-2020), so April bloom is regularly exposed to frost; pick a slope with air drainage.
Rain is fairly even (3.2-4.9 in per month) but July highs average 87 F; drip irrigation is suggested for Piedmont clays during dry spells.
Spacing: semi-dwarf 12-20 ft in row, 15-20 ft between rows; dwarf 4-10 ft by 10-15 ft.
Thin to one fruit every 6-8 in at nickel size; train to a central leader with wide crotch angles; prune in late winter.
Sanitation (remove dead wood, mummies and drops; disinfect pruners between trees) plus a regular preventive spray program is the realistic baseline for apples in the Piedmont.
Local fruit-tree source: Alexander County Extension's annual fruit plant sale in Taylorsville. No Statesville garden centre carrying apple trees was verified.
